https://www.politico.eu/article/friedric.text: BERLIN — Friedrich Merz faces a stark choice: Reshape the unpopular reform drive on which he has staked his chancellorship — or risk going down defending it. The day after his conservatives’ worst election defeat in postwar German history and the far-right Alternative for Germany party’s second win in two weeks in votes in the east of the country, Merz acknowledged that the German public’s rejection of his reform drive was a big part of his party’s problem. But he exhibited no clear plan for what to do about it. Leaders from Merz’s Christian Democratic Union publicly closed ranks around the chancellor and his reform drive on Monday, despite growing internal concern that his leadership is rapidly driving their party toward demise. Advertisement Advertisement In truth, they have little choice. The alternative — an attempt to replace him — is too divisive and risky at a time when the AfD is leading in polls , and the Kremlin is threatening Europe in increasingly aggressive terms. Merz suggested he recognized the scale of the alarm inside his party. “This is a severe blow, and its repercussions will be felt for a long time,” Merz said of the result in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the CDU crashed out of the state parliament with just 4.9% of the vote. But then the chancellor offered little more than a promise to come up with a plan — saying he had scheduled meetings with CDU leaders and state premiers in the coming days to discuss how they should chart a new course. “We want to move the reform process forward, but we know that we also owe the people answers to their concerns and fears,” he said. “Many people are worried about their jobs, worried about their families, worried about their retirement income, and worried about health care. It is the historic task of the coalition here in Berlin — and of the political center as a whole — to prepare our country to face all these challenges in the years ahead.” Economists argue the reforms Merz wants, such as overhauls of the public pension and healthcare schemes to make them more sustainable as the country’s population rapidly ages and costs skyrocket, are essential to reviving Germany’s competitiveness. Advertisement Advertisement Whereas previous governments avoided tackling such reforms due to the political perils of measures like raising the retirement age and trimming health insurance benefits, Merz has embraced the task. He has dubbed himself the “reform chancellor” and argues that he’s tackling a generational task on par with rebuilding Germany after World War II. But voters view the reform drive — and the way Merz has often taken a lecturing tone when promoting its necessity — in overwhelmingly negative terms. In late August, a survey by the Hans Böckler Foundation of the German labor union association found that about 81 percent of respondents were concerned about their financial security as a result of the government’s reform push. The same poll found 42 percent were cutting back on their consumer spending as a result of those fears. This is a problem that CDU leaders now admit. “Right now, our platform isn’t appealing to many people,” CDU Education Minister Karin Prien told a German public television interviewer Monday even as she argued there was no way around structural reforms. No better alternative On Monday, Merz again moved to quell suggestions he would step aside in a so-called Kanzlertausch — or chancellor swap. Advertisement Advertisement “Neither last night nor this morning did anyone raise any personnel-related questions, let alone engage in a debate on personnel matters. Not a single person,” Merz told reporters in Berlin. Prien was among the CDU leaders who publicly closed ranks — but, notably, her endorsement of the chancellor was not exactly glowing. Prien suggested Merz would stay on because the party could not agree on who would take the helm. “Our country is in a truly difficult situation, and I’m weighing our options very carefully,” she told German public television Monday. “I don’t see how replacing a leader would actually bring about change, unless there is another candidate available. I don’t see that either. And in that regard, we must now work together with the chancellor — as a government on the one hand and as a party on the other — to discuss how we can regain greater acceptance and credibility among the public.” Two CDU officials, granted anonymity to discuss the party’s internal mood, said upcoming meetings of party leaders, including on Tuesday, when Merz is to face his parliamentary group in the Bundestag, are expected to become tense. But they said Merz is safe as long as his critics in the party can’t agree on the best candidate to succeed him. “It’s always easy to voice criticism,” said one conservative lawmaker. “But after that, you also have to be able to say what comes next — and that’s when things tend to quickly get pretty quiet.” A closed-door meeting of the CDU leaders is also expected to take place next weekend in Berlin. Advertisement Advertisement For many conservatives, attempting a leadership bid at a time of such profound global instability is just too risky. The effort could inadvertently trigger an election or end up strengthening the AfD — now the most popular party in Germany, according to polls — which would certainly render any new chancellor installed without an election democratically illegitimate. Even if Merz clings to power in the short term, more electoral challenges loom. With five regional elections set for next year across Germany, the chancellor and his party need to turn things around quickly. Coalition partner demands its price That makes the question of how Merz will reshape his reform drive all the more important. But the effort to push through reforms isn’t bound to get easier, especially as Merz’s coalition only has a 12-vote majority in the Bundestag — making it vulnerable to even a small defection. On Monday, Merz’s coalition partners in the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) said they would continue to govern with the chancellor’s conservatives, but suggested they would seek an additional price. “If the citizens of our country perceive reforms as something that threatens their lives and only leads to deterioration, then it is not only our communication that needs to improve, but also in some areas the substance of the reforms themselves,” SPD Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said in Berlin on Monday. At the same time, the AfD is piling on pressure on Merz, using his weakness to attack his agenda as well as his party’s “firewall” policy of refusing to govern with the far right — and depicting themselves as the party of true reform. Advertisement Advertisement “We don’t believe the CDU can continue this way,” AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel said Monday in Berlin. “We’ll see what the next few weeks bring. But Germany urgently needs reforms that aren’t being implemented,” she added. “We stand ready.” Merz on Monday depicted his efforts as necessary to ward off the rising political extremes in Germany on both sides of the spectrum, saying his success was linked to the survival of ailing mainstream parties. “It will be a historic task — not only for the current governing coalition here in Berlin, but especially for the party I lead — to ensure that we remain, now and in the future, a united nation and a party that feels firmly anchored in the European Union,” he said. “We must now weather the storms of our time.” Rasmus Buchsteiner contributed reporting

https://telex.hu/english/2026/09/25/hung.text: Menü Kereső Hungary reduces SAFE defence loan request to €5.4 billion English Pál Tamás Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Hungary has requested a loan of 5.4 billion euros (1,973 billion forints) from the European Union’s SAFE defense loan facility, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Régnier announced at a press conference on Friday. The Hungarian government had previously planned to take out a SAFE loan of 16 billion euros, Hvg.hu has reported. At Friday’s press conference, a Euronews reporter asked about the situation with Italy and Hungary, as these are the two countries still awaiting final Commission approval with regard to the SAFE loan. The Commission spokesperson responded by saying that progress had been made in both countries, and that they had received new information and updated plans from both the Italian and Hungarian authorities, which are currently being analyzed. “There will be a bit more than 8 billion euros taken by Italy, and the Hungarian authorities have informed us that they will be taking 5.4 billion euros in the end. We welcome this step. We are in close contact with the Hungarian authorities on the updated plan, which we should receive soon,” said Thomas Régnier, noting that member states can decide how much they wish to borrow, and the European Commission will not reduce the available amounts. When asked why Hungary is now requesting only 5.4 billion euros instead of the originally planned approximately 16 billion euros, the spokesperson replied: “We have always been very clear with the new Hungarian authorities and government that they would, of course, be able to take stock of the current situation. And they have now decided to take less than what we originally allocated to Hungary.” He added that the remaining loan amount of more than 10 billion euros will be reallocated for a later date. HVG points out that the Hungarian government was not the only EU government which decided not to use their entire credit line. Consequently, the European Commission will publish a new call for proposals later this year, allowing member states to apply for the remaining funds. The new call for proposals must be published before 2026 is over- otherwise, the funds would be forfeited. The European Commission proposed a joint loan of up to 150 billion euros last year to help member states develop their defense capabilities and industries. The Hungarian government at the time was the only one not to vote in favor of SAFE in the EU Council of Ministers. Despite this, Minister of Economy Márton Nagy later announced that Hungary had applied for 20 billion euros (8,000 billion forints) from the fund, and the European Commission had allocated 16.2 billion euros (roughly 6,300 billion forints) of that amount—the third-largest allocation in the EU. However, citing the scale of the plan and the necessary bilateral consultations, the European Commission has so far denied approval of the Hungarian plan several times. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/20/uaes.text: As the race to elect the next UN Secretary-General enters its final phase, UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh, who is running to succeed António Guterres, has pledged to serve as the UN's chief mediator and take political risks for peace if chosen for the organisation's top post.Speaking in a wide-ranging interview with Euronews, Nusseibeh, who served as the UAE's ambassador to the UN for more than a decade, said the organisation must get back to its core purpose of bringing governments and people together for peace, development and prosperity to restore its credibility."I think it's a turning point moment for the United Nations," she said."I am a relentless diplomat and I intend to offer a candidacy that is about relentless diplomacy," Nusseibeh told Euronews.Nusseibeh said the UN was too often seen as absent from the 65 active conflicts she said exist worldwide, and that the next secretary-general should act as mediator in chief, pursuing humanitarian truces and aid access first, then a political strategy to make them last."It's not about political theatre, it's about political risk-taking," she said.With official development assistance down 23%, Nusseibeh said the UN would have to narrow its scope, partner with others where they are better placed, and publish a scorecard of results for member states and donors."It's not around organograms or design structures of the system, but it's about impact and cost of impact and delivery," she said.In her first 100 days, she said she would agree on a shared vision with member states and civil society, cut duplication across the thousands of mandates given to the secretariat and move the UN's focus from headquarters to the field.First woman to lead the UN?If chosen, Nusseibeh would become the first woman to lead the UN since its establishment in 1945, the first of Palestinian descent, and the second secretary-general from the Arabic-speaking world after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali."But I'm not running because I'm a woman. I'm running because of over two decades of experience and judgment in international diplomacy," Nusseibeh said.Asked about critics who have questioned her independence, Nusseibeh pointed to the UN Charter. She has taken leave from her post as UAE minister of state to campaign."Article 100 of the UN Charter stipulates the independence of a secretary-general," she said."So the allegiance of a secretary-general is to the UN Charter and to international law and that is what I would pledge in that role," she said."I welcome the criticism, I welcome feedback, I will always welcome the feedback if I am in this role as well," she added.Nusseibeh said the next secretary-general must combine public advocacy for peace with discreet diplomacy."Sometimes quiet diplomacy is needed, keeping channels open to all parties when the doors are closed," she said.She said she would set up a mediation board of outside experts and UN officials, draw on local community leaders and make women's networks the first point of contact for her mediation team. Nusseibeh would also create a focal point in her own office for the protection of aid workers, 300 of whom she said had been killed in the past year."I would continue to try relentlessly until there is an outcome that serves the people on the ground better," she said.Approaching conflict 'with a lot of humility'On Ukraine, she said any settlement must rest on the UN Charter's principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity."I would offer my good offices immediately," she said. "Where that is welcomed, I would come with options, practical options for how to move from first agreements to a political strategy."Nusseibeh said 38% of the Security Council's agenda concerned the Middle East, a region she said had seen generations of war.A fluent Hebrew speaker and a highly regarded diplomat who grew up between Abu Dhabi and the UK in a family of well-known Palestinian political figures, Nusseibeh previously served as the UAE ambassador to the UN and is credited with elevating the UAE's profile during that time."One of my driving purposes in seeking this role is to try and pass on a region that is more stable, more prosperous for my own children," she said.On Gaza, Nusseibeh cited Security Council Resolution 2720, which she negotiated in December 2023 after taking council ambassadors to the Rafah crossing. She said Resolution 2803, which endorsed a 20-point plan for Gaza, had stalled."As Secretary General, I would want to see that through in terms of implementation," she said.Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage with family roots in Jerusalem, said the issue was both professional and personal for her."I come to every conflict with a lot of humility that what we have done in all of these situations has not been nearly enough for the people who've needed it the most," she said.The Security Council has held repeated informal straw polls, with no candidate yet clearing opposition from all five permanent members, and Guterres's term is due to end on 31 December.Race remains tightIn the closely watched UN race, former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan still holds a challenging lead as Argentina’s International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi and UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh actively campaign to emerge as winners.The growing excitement around the race is also fueled by the prospect of a female UN secretary-general, something that has never happened in the UN's more than 80-year history.Campaigning alongside Grynspan, Nusseibeh and Rossi are Guyana’s former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, former Ecuadorian Foreign Minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, former UN Under-Secretary-General Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.Costa Rica's former Vice President Rebeca Grynspan, 70, was born to Jewish parents who fled Poland before World War II. She lost her grandparents in the Holocaust after they decided to remain in Poland.In a May interview with Euronews, Grynspan said, “I know exactly what wars take away from you and what peace allows you to do.”“I am a generation that have lived in peace. I have never experienced war directly. But millions of people in the world today live in war zones, in conflict. And that is why I am running, because I know the difference, what peace and opportunity can do for you and your family,” Grynspan told Euronews at the time.
